analysis.one_liner: Extends the federal nuclear-accident liability backstop for power plant operators.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a Senate committee with no cosponsors and was never voted on.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would renew the federal government's nuclear accident liability program through August 2012, a decade past its scheduled expiration. That program requires nuclear plant operators to carry insurance, pools their payments after an accident, and has the federal government stand behind them for losses beyond that pool. It would also double the maximum annual premium that can be charged back to a plant owner following an accident, from $10 million to $20 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Nuclear power plant operators gain the most: the federal backstop that limits their exposure to catastrophic accident costs would continue through 2012, and accident victims keep the guaranteed compensation system the program funds. The general public retains a defined system for paying damages if a plant accident occurs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nuclear plant operators and accident victims

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's authority to indemnify (back up) its licensees from August 1, 2002 to August 1, 2012, keeping the federal nuclear liability program in force for another decade.

Doubles the maximum deferred premium that can be charged to a plant owner following a nuclear incident, from $10 million to $20 million per year per facility, increasing the money operators contribute after an accident.
Keeps a defined compensation system in place so that people harmed in a nuclear accident have a guaranteed pool of funds rather than depending on a plant owner's solvency.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the ultimate backstop: losses beyond the industry-funded insurance pool could fall on the federal government. Plant owners also face higher potential annual premiums after an accident.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, as the ultimate loss backstop

drawbacks.text: The federal government remains the backstop for catastrophic nuclear losses beyond the industry-funded pool, so the largest costs of a severe accident could ultimately land on taxpayers.

Doubling the deferred premium to $20 million a year is still small relative to the potential scale of a major nuclear accident, leaving a wide gap between what operators can be charged and what a catastrophe could cost.
The bill only extends Congress's required oversight reports to 2008, limiting how long lawmakers would be forced to formally review how the program is performing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a routine extension of a decades-old liability system that guarantees accident victims a compensation pool while limiting plant owners' downside. The tradeoff is real but tail-risk-shaped: in any ordinary year it costs nothing, but a severe accident could shift enormous losses to the federal government. Doubling the post-accident premium only partially narrows that gap.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator James Inhofe introduced the bill on March 23, 2000, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: nuclear plant operators kept the existing liability backstop on its current terms through 2002, without the doubled premium or the longer extension. The public gained nothing from the guaranteed compensation extension but also took on no new federal exposure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nuclear plant operators, who kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up; it received no hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action in the more than nine months between its referral and the end of the session.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or roll calls occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Nuclear power plant owners and operators
industries.note: The bill locks in the federal liability backstop that caps operators' downside for catastrophic accidents while guaranteeing a compensation pool for victims. Operators would also face a higher post-accident charge, up to $20 million a year per facility, a real but small cost compared to what a severe accident could run.

industries.industry: Nuclear insurers and the insurance market for nuclear facilities
industries.note: Extending the liability program keeps the federal requirement that licensees carry primary financial protection, sustaining the market for nuclear insurance and the guarantee that accident victims can be paid.

Taxpayers stand behind the program for losses beyond the industry-funded pool, a contingent liability with no cost unless a major accident occurs. The extension also keeps a compensation system funded by operators and premiums rather than an unfunded disaster gap.
